config.title: Multi-Step Form

intro.title: Multi-Step Form
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a multi-step form that guides users through a sign-up process in distinct stages, such as entering personal details, setting preferences, and confirming their submission. You will learn how to manage form state and navigation between steps using React's useState hook to track the current step and user inputs. The core programming concept involves conditional rendering to display different form sections based on the active step, along with event handlers to move forward and backward. You'll implement this in TypeScript with React components, ensuring type safety for form data and a structured, user-friendly interface.
intro.usecase: Multi-step forms are essential in real-world applications where complex data collection needs to be broken down into manageable chunks. You'll find them in e-commerce checkout processes, user onboarding flows, insurance quote generators, and financial service applications. These forms improve user experience by reducing cognitive overload and guiding users through logical sequences. As a developer, you'll implement these patterns for sign-up wizards, multi-page surveys, and complex configuration interfaces where data validation and user progress tracking are critical.

objectives: Define a TypeScript interface to structure form data with multiple fields across steps
Implement useState hooks to manage form data and track the current step
Apply conditional rendering to display different form sections based on the current step
Construct a component structure with separate sections for each step of the form
Utilize event handlers to update form data when input values change
Control navigation between steps with functions that increment and decrement the step counter
Execute validation logic to check required fields before allowing progression to the next step
Implement a progress indicator component that visually represents the current step
Use props to pass form data and handlers between parent and child form step components
Return a complete multi-step form component with all navigation and data flow functionality

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added to the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using the import syntax.

steps.title: Create the MultiStepForm component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named MultiStepForm that returns null for now. Use TypeScript syntax.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Make sure to export it.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the MultiStepForm component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named MultiStepForm is created and exported, returning null.
successCriteria: The component is defined with the correct name, returns null, and is exported.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the MultiStepForm component. This is the foundation for our multi-step form.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named exactly 'MultiStepForm', returns null, and is exported.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on creating just the component. Create a function named MultiStepForm that returns null and export it.

steps.title: Define the form steps as an array
steps.instruction: Inside your MultiStepForm component, define a constant array named 'steps' that contains string titles for each step of your form (e.g., 'Personal Info', 'Contact Details', 'Confirmation').
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword to create an array of strings. Place this definition inside the component function body, before the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a 'steps' array defined inside your component with at least two string elements representing form step titles.
successCriteria: The code must include a constant named 'steps' defined inside the MultiStepForm component, containing an array of strings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the steps array that will track the different stages of your multi-step form.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a constant named 'steps' with an array of strings inside the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The steps array definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a constant named 'steps' with an array of string titles inside your component.

steps.title: Initialize current step state
steps.instruction: Inside the MultiStepForm component, initialize a state variable called 'currentStep' using useState. Set its initial value to 0.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The state should track which step the user is currently on, starting from step 0.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'currentStep' initialized to 0, ready to track which form step the user is viewing.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that declares a 'currentStep' variable with initial value 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the currentStep state. This will allow us to track which step of the form the user is currently viewing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a state variable called 'currentStep' with an initial value of 0. Check that you've spelled everything correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The currentStep state hasn't been initialized correctly. You need to use useState to create a state variable that tracks the current step index, starting at 0.

steps.title: Create handler for next step
steps.instruction: Inside your MultiStepForm component, create a function named handleNext that increments the currentStep state when called, but only if currentStep is less than the last index of the steps array.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses the setCurrentStep updater from useState. You'll need to check if currentStep is less than steps.length - 1 before incrementing.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleNext function is defined that will advance to the next step when called, respecting the boundaries of the steps array.
successCriteria: Function uses setCurrentStep to update state
Function checks if currentStep < steps.length - 1 before incrementing
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the handleNext function. This function will allow users to navigate forward through your form steps while preventing them from going beyond the last step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your handleNext function properly checks if there's a next step available (currentStep < steps.length - 1) before calling setCurrentStep to increment the value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleNext function needs to be defined inside the component. It should check if currentStep is less than steps.length - 1, then use setCurrentStep to increment the step number.

steps.title: Create handler for previous step
steps.instruction: Inside the MultiStepForm component, create a function named handlePrevious that decrements the currentStep state when called, but only if currentStep is greater than 0.
steps.hint: Define a function that checks if currentStep > 0 before calling setCurrentStep with currentStep - 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a handlePrevious function that safely decrements the current step when called, preventing going below step 0.
successCriteria: The handlePrevious function should be defined, check if currentStep > 0, and call setCurrentStep with currentStep - 1 when the condition is true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a handlePrevious function that safely navigates to the previous step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your handlePrevious function checks if currentStep > 0 before decrementing, and calls setCurrentStep with the updated value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handlePrevious function isn't quite right. It should check if currentStep > 0 and then decrement the step using setCurrentStep.

steps.title: Return a container div
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a container div element that wraps the existing content.
steps.hint: The div should surround the existing h1 element to create a proper container structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div element that contains the h1 heading.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div element
The div wraps the existing h1 element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a container div that properly wraps the form content.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning a div element that contains the h1 heading.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're returning a div element with the h1 inside it in the return statement.

steps.title: Add step indicator display
steps.instruction:
Inside the return statement of your MultiStepForm component, add a paragraph (

) element that displays the current step number and total number of steps. Use the format 'Step X of Y', where X is the current step number (starting from 1) and Y is the total number of steps.
steps.hint: You can use template literals or string concatenation to combine the currentStep state (add 1 to show 1-based numbering) and the steps array length.
steps.expectedOutcome: A paragraph element showing the current step progress (e.g., 'Step 1 of 3') will appear below the heading in the rendered form.
successCriteria: The paragraph must display the correct current step number (1-based) and total steps count using the existing currentStep state and steps array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a step indicator that shows the user's progress through the form. This provides important visual feedback about where they are in the multi-step process.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be an issue with the step numbering or the total count. Make sure you're displaying the current step as a 1-based number (currentStep + 1) and the total from the steps array length.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step indicator isn't displaying correctly. Check that you've added a paragraph element with the current step number and total steps. Remember to use the existing currentStep state and steps array variables.

steps.title: Add step title display
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement, add a heading (h2) that displays the title of the current step from the steps array. Use the currentStep state as the index to access the correct step title.
steps.hint: You can access the current step title with steps[currentStep]. Add an h2 element containing this value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will display the current step's title (e.g., 'Step 1', 'Step 2', or 'Step 3') in an h2 heading below the main title.
successCriteria: The code includes an h2 element that renders the current step title from the steps array using the currentStep state as index.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a heading that displays the current step title. The form now shows which step the user is on.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be a small issue. Make sure you're using steps[currentStep] inside an h2 element to display the current step title.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't seem quite right. Remember to add an h2 element that displays the current step title from the steps array using currentStep as the index.

steps.title: Add Previous button with click handler
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your MultiStepForm component, add a button element with the text 'Previous' and wire its onClick event to call the handlePrevious function.
steps.hint: Remember to use the onClick prop and pass the handlePrevious function reference without calling it (e.g., onClick={handlePrevious}).
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'Previous' button appears in the form that, when clicked, will eventually navigate to the previous step (once handlePrevious is implemented).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the Previous button with its click handler wired up. This will allow users to navigate backward through the form steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both the button with 'Previous' text AND the onClick handler set to handlePrevious.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or its click handler isn't quite right. Check that you have a button element with the text 'Previous' and its onClick prop set to handlePrevious.

steps.title: Add Next button with click handler
steps.instruction: Add a Next button inside the return statement of your MultiStepForm component. The button should display 'Next' and call the handleNext function when clicked. Use a ternary operator to change the button text to 'Submit' when the current step is the last step (currentStep === steps.length - 1).
steps.hint: Place the button after the Previous button in your JSX. Use onClick={handleNext} and conditionally set the button text.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Next button appears after the Previous button. The button text changes to 'Submit' on the last step. Clicking the button triggers the handleNext function.
successCriteria: The Next button is added with onClick={handleNext}. The button text uses a ternary to show 'Submit' on the last step, 'Next' otherwise.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the Next button with conditional text and wired it to the handleNext function. This completes the basic navigation for your multi-step form.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a Next button, but check: Did you wire onClick to handleNext? Did you use a ternary to conditionally show 'Submit' on the last step?
steps.feedbackWrong: The Next button is missing or incorrect. Ensure you add a <button> element with onClick={handleNext} and conditionally set its text using a ternary operator based on currentStep.

steps.title: Export the component
steps.instruction: Export the MultiStepForm component as the default export.
steps.hint: At the bottom of the file, use 'export default MultiStepForm' to make the component available for import in other files.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MultiStepForm component is now available for import in other files via default export.
successCriteria: The component is exported as default using 'export default MultiStepForm'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the MultiStepForm component as default. This makes it ready to be imported and used in other parts of your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're exporting the MultiStepForm component as the default export using 'export default MultiStepForm'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component needs to be exported as default. Use 'export default MultiStepForm' at the end of the file.
